title: Writing your first server action

thumbnail.alt: Video thumbnail for Writing your first server action

children.text: A server action is a function that only ever runs on the server but can be called from the client. It replaces the route handler you would otherwise write by hand.
What this lesson covers
Define an action and call it from a form or an event
Revalidate the affected data after a write
Keep write credentials on the server side of the call
This lesson sits in Server Actions and Mutations, part of Next.js App Router in Depth. It assumes what came before it and leads directly into the next lesson in the module.

keyPoints: Define an action and call it from a form or an event
Revalidate the affected data after a write
Keep write credentials on the server side of the call

title: Forms, validation, and error states

thumbnail.alt: Video thumbnail for Forms, validation, and error states

children.text: Client-side validation is a convenience; the server check is the real one. Parse the payload on arrival and return errors the form can render.
What this lesson covers
Validate submitted data on the server before writing
Return structured field errors back to the form
Keep the form usable when JavaScript has not loaded
This lesson sits in Server Actions and Mutations, part of Next.js App Router in Depth. It assumes what came before it and leads directly into the next lesson in the module.

keyPoints: Validate submitted data on the server before writing
Return structured field errors back to the form
Keep the form usable when JavaScript has not loaded
proTip: Never trust the shape of an incoming payload. Parse it, then use the parsed value.

title: Optimistic updates

children.text: Optimistic UI shows the expected result immediately and reconciles when the server answers. The interesting part is what happens when the server disagrees.
What this lesson covers
Render the expected state before the server confirms
Roll back cleanly when the action fails
Keep optimistic state scoped to the component that owns it
This lesson sits in Server Actions and Mutations, part of Next.js App Router in Depth. It assumes what came before it and leads directly into the next lesson in the module.

keyPoints: Render the expected state before the server confirms
Roll back cleanly when the action fails
Keep optimistic state scoped to the component that owns it

title: Profiling with React DevTools

thumbnail.alt: Video thumbnail for Profiling with React DevTools

children.text: The profiler records what rendered, how long it took, and why it happened. Reading a flame graph correctly is most of the diagnostic work.
What this lesson covers
Record a realistic interaction, not an idle page
Read the flame graph and the ranked chart
Turn on "why did this render" to get the cause
This lesson sits in Measuring Performance, part of React Performance Engineering. It assumes what came before it and leads directly into the next lesson in the module.

keyPoints: Record a realistic interaction, not an idle page
Read the flame graph and the ranked chart
Turn on "why did this render" to get the cause

title: Core Web Vitals in a React app

thumbnail.alt: Video thumbnail for Core Web Vitals in a React app

children.text: Lab numbers on your laptop are not what users experience. Vitals give you a field measure of loading, responsiveness, and visual stability.
What this lesson covers
Interpret LCP, INP, and CLS in practical terms
Separate lab data from field data
Attribute a poor score to a specific element or interaction
This lesson sits in Measuring Performance, part of React Performance Engineering. It assumes what came before it and leads directly into the next lesson in the module.

keyPoints: Interpret LCP, INP, and CLS in practical terms
Separate lab data from field data
Attribute a poor score to a specific element or interaction
proTip: A good score on your machine means very little. Look at the field data from real devices.

title: Finding wasted renders

thumbnail.alt: Video thumbnail for Finding wasted renders

children.text: Most React slowness is a subtree re-rendering for no reason. Track it back to the prop or context value that changes identity on every render.
What this lesson covers
Trace a re-render back to the prop that changed
Spot object and function props recreated each render
Recognise context as a re-render broadcast
This lesson sits in Measuring Performance, part of React Performance Engineering. It assumes what came before it and leads directly into the next lesson in the module.

keyPoints: Trace a re-render back to the prop that changed
Spot object and function props recreated each render
Recognise context as a re-render broadcast

title: When memo actually helps

thumbnail.alt: Video thumbnail for When memo actually helps

children.text: memo skips a re-render when props are shallow-equal. It costs a comparison on every render, so applying it everywhere makes things slower, not faster.
What this lesson covers
Apply memo to expensive subtrees with stable props
Understand shallow comparison and why objects defeat it
Recognise when restructuring beats memoising
This lesson sits in Rendering Optimization, part of React Performance Engineering. It assumes what came before it and leads directly into the next lesson in the module.

keyPoints: Apply memo to expensive subtrees with stable props
Understand shallow comparison and why objects defeat it
Recognise when restructuring beats memoising

title: useMemo and useCallback in practice

thumbnail.alt: Video thumbnail for useMemo and useCallback in practice

children.text: These hooks preserve identity between renders. Their value is in what depends on that identity, not in the caching itself.
What this lesson covers
Memoise values that feed memoised children or effects
Get the dependency array right, every time
Skip memoisation when the computation is trivial
This lesson sits in Rendering Optimization, part of React Performance Engineering. It assumes what came before it and leads directly into the next lesson in the module.

keyPoints: Memoise values that feed memoised children or effects
Get the dependency array right, every time
Skip memoisation when the computation is trivial
proTip: If nothing downstream depends on the identity of a value, memoising it buys you nothing.

title: Keys and list reconciliation

thumbnail.alt: Video thumbnail for Keys and list reconciliation

children.text: Keys tell React which item is which. Using an array index means insertions silently reassign state to the wrong row.
What this lesson covers
Use stable identity for keys, never the array index
Understand how reconciliation matches elements between renders
Diagnose lost input state in a reordered list
This lesson sits in Rendering Optimization, part of React Performance Engineering. It assumes what came before it and leads directly into the next lesson in the module.

keyPoints: Use stable identity for keys, never the array index
Understand how reconciliation matches elements between renders
Diagnose lost input state in a reordered list
